newsitem.title: UK: Options market in the dark on NatWest charge.
newsitem.headline: Options market in the dark on NatWest charge.

text.p: National Westminster Bank Plc's disclosure late on Friday that it would make a 50 million pounds ($81.4 million) provision for options mispricing errors took London's financial derivatives market by surprise.
Dealers were left guessing who was behind the transactions that led to the provision or whether they took place on an exchange or the over the counter options market.
The London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange (LIFFE), the site for a large part of London's options trading, had no immediate comment on the news.
NatWest said on Friday it had found mispricing errors in the interest rate options book of its Natwest Markets unit, and the group would be making a provision of 50 million stg.

"A senior trader has been suspended for failure to supervise, pending the conclusion of an internal inquiry," NatWest said in a statement, adding it had reported a second trader who had left the firm to the Securities & Futures Authority (SFA) regulator.
Dealers and industry figures said mispricing could arise in various ways. For instance, a broker could be given a price from clients but somehow get the price wrong in executing the trade.
One options dealer added the situation also could be down to how an individual dealt with issues such as margins on his firm's trades.
"Basically if you're a senior trader or a top person you can actually change prices or positions for margining," the dealer said.
He and other traders said they did not know who was at the heart of the affair.

Options are contracts which give buyers the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell an underlying security at a set price in the future. A "call" gives a buyer the right to purchase something while a "put" gives one the right to sell at specific prices.
Mispricing errors are not unheard of in the options market, which is one of the more sophisticated of the derivatives markets. But one trader said the provision in this case was unusually large.
"50 million stg is a good size," he said.
Another trader at a European house said he he was surprised that NatWest may have made such pricing mistakes.
"I've had dealings with NatWest and their group is very good so this is a surprise to me," the trader said.
NatWest said the Bank of England was being kept informed. A Bank of England spokesman confirmed this but declined to comment further.
Deriviatves markets have been involved in a string of large losses for companies around the world. The most famous cases include the collapse of Barings under the weight some $1.4 billion.
